original_value: Network traffic exhibits a high level of variability over short periods of time. This variability impacts negatively on the accuracy of anomaly-based network intrusion detection systems (IDS) that are built using predictive models in a batch learning setup. This work investigates how adapting the discriminating threshold of model predictions, specifically to the evaluated traffic, improves the detection rates of these intrusion detection models. Specifically, this research studied the adaptability features of three well known machine learning algorithms: C5.0, Random Forest and Support Vector Machine. Each algorithm’s ability to adapt their prediction thresholds was assessed and analysed under different scenarios that simulated real world settings using the prospective sampling approach. Multiple IDS datasets were used for the analysis, including a newly generated dataset (STA2018). This research demonstrated empirically the importance of threshold adaptation in improving the accuracy of detection models when training and evaluation traffic have different statistical properties. Tests were undertaken to analyse the effects of feature selection and data balancing on model accuracy when different significant features in traffic were used. The effects of threshold adaptation on improving accuracy were statistically analysed. Of the three compared algorithms, Random Forest was the most adaptable and had the highest detection rates.

result.paraphrase: Network traffic can vary greatly over short time spans, and this variability reduces the accuracy of anomaly-based network intrusion detection systems built from predictive models in a batch-learning setting. This study examines whether adapting the decision threshold of model predictions to the evaluated traffic can improve the detection rates of these IDS models. In particular, it analyzed the threshold-adaptation capabilities of three well-known machine learning algorithms: C5.0, Random Forest, and Support Vector Machine. Each algorithm’s ability to adjust its prediction thresholds was evaluated and compared under different scenarios simulating real-world conditions using the prospective sampling approach. The analysis used multiple IDS datasets, including a newly created dataset, STA2018. The research empirically showed that threshold adaptation is important for improving detection-model accuracy when training and evaluation traffic have different statistical properties. Tests also examined how feature selection and data balancing affected model accuracy when different significant traffic features were used. The impact of threshold adaptation on accuracy improvement was statistically analyzed. Among the three algorithms compared, Random Forest was the most adaptable and achieved the highest detection rates.
